lines.text: Before the reveal, think about this from the system's point of view: the pile of runs only grows, and every read gets a little slower for it.
What's actually worth doing about that, given that rewriting data costs real disk time too?
Not nothing, and not everything at once either — some runs get merged together, on a schedule, trading some disk time now for a cheaper read later.
Merging on every single flush would mean paying that rewrite cost constantly, which defeats the entire point of writing sequentially in the first place.
One scheme keeps each level down to exactly one sorted run, with a size limit attached to it.
Once a level outgrows that limit, its run gets folded into the next level down, and that fold rewrites every key it touches, not just the new ones.
The upside is that a lookup never has more than one run per level to check — the downside is a key can get rewritten again and again as it works its way down.
A different scheme lets several similarly sized runs just sit there, side by side, completely unmerged.
Only once enough of them have piled up does the whole batch get folded together into one wider run.
A key barely gets touched this way, which is cheap — but now a lookup has to check every one of those unmerged runs instead of just one.
Three separate numbers are what actually let you compare these two schemes honestly, instead of arguing from intuition.
One counts the extra bytes a disk ends up writing beyond the single logical write that caused them.
Another counts the extra runs a lookup has to open beyond the one that actually holds the answer, and the third counts the extra bytes sitting on disk beyond what the live data alone would need.
Before the reveal, here's the real question: given that one scheme above is clearly cheaper to read from and the other is clearly cheaper to write to, can some clever design just win on every count?
No. Pinning down any two of those three numbers forces the third one upward — there's no way around it, only a choice of which one gets to be the loser.
A hybrid scheme doesn't escape that. It's still built from the same two moves, so it just inherits a share of both costs instead of neither.
So here's the actual shape of the trade: one scheme wins by keeping wasted disk space down, at the cost of extra reading and extra rewriting.
The other wins by keeping rewriting down, at the cost of extra reading and extra wasted space.
Splitting the difference, tiered near the top and the other scheme near the bottom, doesn't dodge this — it just picks a different spot on the exact same curve.
There's a piece of this that's tunable completely separately from which merging scheme you picked at all: how much memory goes to each level's own membership filter.
Most systems just hand every level the same share, measured per key, which sounds fair but isn't actually the cheapest way to spend that memory.
A smarter split gives a small level a stingier wrong-guess rate and a huge level a more generous one, because tightening a filter on a small level buys back far more lookup cost per byte spent.
One more idea pushes this further: treat the two merging schemes not as a binary choice but as opposite ends of one continuous line.
Then pick a point on that line based on the actual shape of a given workload, merging aggressively only where it actually pays for itself.
That doesn't make the underlying trade go away. It just means someone found a better spot on it than guessing would have.
Here's what actually got measured, not assumed: write, read, and wasted-space cost for both merging schemes, run on the exact same sequence of inserts and updates.
Also measured: how much a smarter, per-level split of filter memory beats an equal-everywhere split, at the identical total memory budget.
